sections.html: The small spiny eel Macrognathus aculeatus rarely grows to 20 cm long, even though 38 cm is given as the maximum length in the literature. It is one of the longest known species of these bizarre fishes. The care of these animals is easy.

The species was described by Bloch in 1786. As so often with long-known species, there are many misidentifications in the literature, because the origin was only vaguely known to Bloch; he gives "East India", which at that time corresponded to the Moluccas, the Indonesian island world and the Malacca peninsula. In this area there are several similar Macrognathus species. Therefore Kottelat and Widjanarti limited the origin to Java in 2005 and established a neotype from there as future reference.

Apparently adult Macrognathus (the females show clear spawning condition) were imported from Indonesia which, according to the exporter, were collected on the relatively small island of Bangka. Bangka is located east off Sumatra and about 500 km north of Java. These spiny eels are not distinguishable from the neotype and are perhaps the first "real" Macrognathus aculeatus that came alive to Germany, at least recognized as such.
In nature they seem to colonize peat swamps with strongly acidic blackwater.

Temperature requirements are between 22 and 28°C. Although in nature they seem to colonize peat swamps with strongly acidic blackwater, they adapt well to "normal" water conditions. Any drinking-quality tap water is suitable for their care.
It is best to give frozen and live food. They prefer red mosquito larvae (bloodworms), tubifex and the like. After acclimation they usually also accept granulated food.
They are peaceful, sociable fish that like to cuddle with conspecifics in a lair. However, small fish are seen as a food supplement, so attention should be paid to this.
The sexes differ mainly in the abdominal girth, which is considerably fuller in females.
All spiny eels are free spawners, spawning near the water surface in dense plant tangles.
